name: Grafton
headline: Grafton, village by village,
from the common to the river.
answer: Grafton is a Worcester County town of 19,664 people (2020 Census) bordering Worcester, established in 1735. Its housing runs from the 19th-century homes around Grafton Common to worker housing in its Blackstone River mill villages. Grafton station in North Grafton is on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line, and Routes 122, 140 and 30 cross the town.
overview: Grafton's story begins with Hassanamisco, a Christian Indian plantation established in 1654; the town itself was established in 1735. Hassanamesitt Woods, about 200 acres on Keith Hill, is believed to hold the core of that Nipmuc village, and the Trust for Public Land bought it in 2004 for transfer to the town. Grafton Common was landscaped into an elliptical park in 1843 and 1844; the state's 1984 survey records a temple-front store on the common that became a bank, a mansard-roofed store and residence facing it, and a brick Second Empire block of 1862 to 1863 that served as the town hall.

Away from the common, Grafton spreads into villages built on water power. North Grafton, once New England Village, sits where the Quinsigamond River falls more than 50 feet in a short distance, and Saundersville, Fisherville and Farnumsville line the Blackstone River in the southwest. Benjamin Willard began making clocks in a North Grafton workshop in 1766, a legacy now kept at the Willard House and Clock Museum. Grafton station on Pine Street puts the town on the Framingham/Worcester Line, and Tufts University's Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine has its campus here.

Grafton's zoning already makes room for denser housing near the station: its bylaw includes the North Grafton Transit Village Overlay District, which the town amends under the state's Chapter 40R smart growth rules, and a Village and Neighborhood Mixed Use district. The May 12, 2025 Annual Town Meeting warrant carried amendments to both, including a definition of attached single-family dwellings, such as townhouses and rowhouses, for the mixed-use district. The state lists Grafton as compliant with the MBTA Communities law as of October 21, 2026. Values have climbed: the town reports that the average single-family assessed value rose from $625,767 in FY2025 to $663,695 in FY2026.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's 1984 survey describes Grafton Center as possibly the best-preserved and most substantial 19th-century residential and institutional village in its study area. In the Blackstone River mill villages, double-chimney multi-family worker housing continued to be built, and Farnumsville and Fisherville keep late 19th-century boardinghouses and a few double-deckers; North Grafton has four-unit tenement rows on Second Street. One-story Craftsman bungalows followed, mostly near the villages.

commute.text: Grafton station sits between Worcester and Westborough on the Framingham/Worcester Line, with a 382-space parking lot. Route 140 runs through Grafton Center, Route 122 crosses toward Worcester and Providence, and Route 30 links North Grafton with Westborough.

places.name: Grafton Common
places.line: The town's central green, landscaped as an elliptical park in 1843 and 1844 and framed by 19th-century buildings.

places.name: Willard House and Clock Museum
places.line: The Willard clockmakers' home at 11 Willard Street, North Grafton, showing more than 90 Willard clocks by guided tour.

places.name: Hassanamesitt Woods
places.line: About 200 wooded acres on Keith Hill, believed to hold the core of the 17th-century Nipmuc village, with trails used for hiking, cross-country skiing, horseback riding and birdwatching.

places.name: Grafton Land Trust properties
places.line: The trust lists 26 protected properties, including the Brigham Hill Wildlife Area, Fletcher Reserve and Williams Woods.

places.name: Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine
places.line: Tufts University's veterinary school, on part of the former Grafton State Hospital campus.

places.name: Grafton Inn
places.line: A three-story, five-bay hip-roofed building that Samuel Wood built in 1805, one of the landmarks of Grafton Center.

history.text: The Christian Indian plantation of Hassanamisco was established.
Incorporated as the Town of Grafton.
Benjamin Willard began making clocks in his North Grafton workshop.
The Blackstone Canal was completed, with three locks in Grafton, spurring mill growth along the river.
The Providence and Worcester Railroad began service through the Blackstone River villages in the southwest of town.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Grafton, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Grafton for calendar year 2025 was $610,000, across 153 sales, unchanged from $610,000 in 2024, according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Grafton, MA?
faq.a: Grafton's FY2026 residential tax rate is $13.69 per $1,000 of assessed value, down $0.25 from FY2025, according to the town's State of the Town message. The town reports an average single-family assessed value of $663,695 for FY2026.

faq.q: What kinds of housing are in Grafton?
faq.a: Grafton Center keeps a large stock of 19th-century houses and civic buildings, and the Blackstone River mill villages keep 19th-century multi-family worker housing, boardinghouses and a few double-deckers, according to the state's historic survey. The town reports an average single-family assessed value of $663,695 for FY2026.

notes: Condo rows could not be read (both condo fetches truncated at 'BROOKLI'), so condo fields are null. The MHC town report dates from 1984 and warns that it is dated; its route descriptions (Routes 122, 140, 30) and village character are historic. I could not confirm that I-90 passes through Grafton (the Turnpike exit list names Millbury and Westborough only), so it is left out. Hassanamesitt Woods was bought by the Trust for Public Land in 2004 for transfer to the town; I did not confirm the transfer was completed. Grafton Land Trust acreage is not stated on its site. The district's DESE name is 'Grafton'; 'Grafton Public Schools' is the common name. Deepened 2026-10-22: added a third overview paragraph and rewrote the housing text from the 2018 Housing Production Plan (https://www.mass.gov/doc/grafton-plan/download; structure types, tenure and 7,179 units from 2012 to 2016 ACS; 3,570 units built before 1980; SHI 365 units, 5.1%, date of SHI data not stated). The plan itself flags that its 2016 unit total looks low against permit activity. No newer Grafton HPP was found. Zoning districts and the May 12, 2025 warrant articles (Articles 31 and 32) from https://www.grafton-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/16319/Spring-2025-Warrant_Final; whether those articles passed was not confirmed, and the overview says only that the warrant carried them. MBTA Communities: the state's compliance list 'As of October 21, 2026' includes no. 46 Grafton (https://www.mass.gov/doc/mbta-communities-district-compliance-letters/download); which district the state approved and when was not found, so the record does not say the 40R district is the compliance district. Assessed values and the FY2026 rate from the FY2026 State of the Town message in the April 29, 2026 Finance Committee packet (https://grafton-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/20064/FC-Packet-42926?bidId=), marked preliminary draft; MMA's profile shows $13.94 with no fiscal year (it matches FY2025 per the packet). Added the Grafton Inn (MHC report; current use not stated) to places and history entries 1828 and 1847 from the MHC report. Hassanamisco Reservation is named on Wikipedia but was not added as a place: no source describing the site itself was opened, and the record already covers Hassanamisco's history. Fact-check 2026-10-22 (independent): Verified: population 19,664, three ZIP-code villages and the Worcester border (Wikipedia); MHC report facts (Hassanamisco 1654, 1735, common 1843 to 1844, New England Village in North Grafton and the 50-foot fall, Factory and Second Street worker housing, Blackstone villages in the southwest, Saundersville mill 1829, Centerville west of the center, canal 1828 with three locks, Providence and Worcester Railroad 1847, Grafton Inn 1805, Routes 122, 140 and 30); Grafton station at 1 Pine Street with 382 spaces (MBTA); Willard House at 11 Willard Street, 90+ clocks, guided tours, 1766; Hassanamesitt Woods (TPL, February 17, 2004); Grafton Land Trust list (26 properties); May 12, 2025 warrant, Articles 31 (VMU, attached single-family definition) and 32 (NGTVOD, amended to meet a c. 40R requirement); Grafton compliant, no. 46 (mass.gov list as of October 21, 2026); assessed values $625,767 to $663,695 and the $13.69 rate (FC packet). Tax rate: the only source opened is the April 29, 2026 State of the Town message, headed 'PRELIMINARY DRAFT FOR FINCOM REVIEW', which states in the past tense that 'the tax rate was $13.69 per thousand of value, down $0.25 per thousand from FY2025' (FY2025 $13.94 per BMN Boston and MMA); the draft label applies to the message's wording, and the FY2026 rate would have been set months earlier, so the figure is kept but marked in the tax note as not yet confirmed against DLS. The DLS Databank and the town site's search did not render; no assessor page was found. Corrected: the 40R and transit overlay are one district, not two (the warrant ties the NGTVOD amendment to c. 40R); the common's buildings are now attributed to the 1984 survey rather than said to stand 'still'; the Cummings School is placed on the former Grafton State Hospital campus as Wikipedia says (North Grafton not stated there); Hassanamesitt trail uses now match TPL. Removed: all 2018 Housing Production Plan figures (7,179 units, structure-type shares, 72.3% owner occupied, 3,570 units before 1980, SHI 365 units or 5.1%): the plan PDF on mass.gov returned only binary data in four attempts, no other copy was found, and the 2013 draft figures reported by Patch differ, so none could be confirmed this session; the housing text and FAQ now rest on the MHC report and the town's assessed values. Also removed 'duplexes' and 'Colonial Revival homes' (the MHC report describes double-chimney multi-family worker housing and names only a Colonial Revival police station). Still unconfirmed: the HPP figures above (restore them if the PDF can be read), the FY2026 rate against DLS, the commercial rate, whether Articles 31 and 32 passed, and which district the state approved for MBTA Communities compliance.
